text: Alnham is a hamlet and civil parish in Northumberland, England, located about 14 miles (23 km) west of Alnwick and approximately 6 miles (10 km) from the Scottish border, situated on the south side of a small tributary of the River Alnham. The village lies on uneven ground, sloping from south to north, at the foot of the southern outliers of the Cheviot Hills, with the River Alnham flowing eastward through it from its source in the Cheviot Hills to the coast. The village's layout is influenced by the river. The 2011 Census estimated the population at around 245. Evidence of human occupation in Alnham and its surroundings dates back to prehistoric times, with a cup-marked stone found at Alnham Northfield indicating Neolithic habitation. Bronze Age occupation is evident through a rare bronze spearhead found at High Bleakhope, possibly indicating elite presence, and the spearhead may have been placed as an offering to a deity due to the site's remote and elevated position. Numerous cairns and unenclosed settlements are found in the surrounding area, and two Iron Age palisaded enclosures have been discovered on High Knowes. Castle Hill, a Cheviot multivallate hillfort, is an Iron Age site located to the west of Alnham, standing at 289 metres (948 ft) above Ordnance Datum, with a sub-circular enclosure and ramparts made of earth and stone, and at least five hut circles within it. Three unenclosed huts on the north-west flanks may date from the Bronze Age. The site shows at least four phases of development, beginning with a univallate stone-walled enclosure, followed by bivallate and then multivallate forms. There is also evidence of Romano-British settlement and agricultural activity, including prehistoric cord rig. The name "Alnham" comes from Old English hām (homestead) and the Celtic river-name Aln or Alaunos, meaning "homestead on the River Aln," with recorded variations including Alneham (1331), Elnam (1509), Ayneham (1557), and Ailnham (1663); it has also been historically known as "Yeldom" and in the Magna Britannia of 1724 as "Yarwell." Alnham was part of the Barony of Alnwick held by the Vesci family from the early 12th century until 1310, when it was sold to Henry de Percy, 1st Baron Percy, and has remained in the Percy family since. The Church of St Michael and All Angels, a Grade I listed building and part of the Diocese of Newcastle, was first recorded in an 1184 charter when William de Vesci granted it to Alnwick Abbey; it was later restored in the 13th century and again in 1664 and 1953. The church was damaged during Anglo-Scottish border conflicts and was in a ruinous state by the mid-1800s, with a detailed 1862 description noting damp, mildewed walls, rotting windows, and fungi. F. R. Wilson restored the church in 1870, and Gustav Adolph Renwick carried out further work in 1953. A medieval cross base, 2 feet (61 cm) high and Grade II listed, is located about 20 yards (18 m) south of the church. Tower House, also Grade II listed, was first recorded in 1541 as a "lytle toure" and served as the vicarage; it collapsed in 1651 and remained uninhabitable until 1844, when it was rebuilt with new battlements, turrets, and a residential wing. It is now a private residence. The medieval settlement at Alnham is a scheduled monument located south of St Michaels Church, consisting of earthworks, a toft, two houses, a small hill, and a group of three houses and an enclosure, likely originally larger and centered on the Church. Alnham Castle, a scheduled monument, includes the remains of a medieval tower house with a rectangular plan measuring 22 metres (72 ft) by 18 metres (59 ft) and up to 2 metres (6.6 ft) high, first mentioned in 1405 as one of Harry Hotspur's strongholds, and situated on a low ridge with a triangular annex to the east and south and a well-defined lynchet bank to the north, likely representing a garden and meadow. The former farmhouses of Alnham Castle, known as Castle Farm, are now the Pennywells—two Grade II listed cottages from the early 18th century—along with a Grade II listed garden wall and adjacent farm buildings (byres, stable, and shelter sheds built between 1830 and 1840), all of which have separate Grade II listings. Alnham has historically been affected by Anglo-Scottish border conflicts, with Scottish raids during Henry VIII's reign described in letters from the Earl of Northumberland in October and November 1532, and the tower reportedly in bad condition by 1541. A 1615 survey noted the village's vulnerability due to its location between the two realms. Alnham was a significant agricultural centre in the early 17th century, with Robert Norton's 1619 map showing four large common fields, 70 acres of arable land, and 168 acres of "Alnham oxe pasture." From the 18th century, the village declined due to land leasing policies that consolidated holdings, with the number of cottages dropping from five in Seymour's Survey of c. 1756 to two farms and three cottages by 1776. Alnham Common was first recorded in 1702 and divided in 1776. The 19th century saw Alnham consist of three farms, a church, a vicarage, a Church of England school (built in 1870), and six cottages, with farming remaining the primary economic activity. The population in 1801 was 233 and declined to 205 by 1891, with the 1831 census showing 45 male residents over 20 as labourers or servants, 8 as employers or professionals, and 15 as "middling sorts." In the 20th century, the only new building was the War Memorial Hall, erected in 1921, and the population gradually declined due to mechanisation and reduced farming incomes. Alnham is part of the North Core Strategy Delivery Area of Northumberland, one of the least populated areas in England with 26 residents per square km compared to the county average of 63. In 2001, the parish of Whittingham and Alnham had a total usual population of 505, and in 2011, Alnham Parish had an estimated population of 245. 20.4% of residents were aged 0–15 and 10.2% were aged 65+, with 100% identifying as white; 68.6% were Christian, and 81.3% of those aged 16–74 were economically active, primarily in agriculture, forestry, and fishing (25.7%). Alnham is part of the Berwick-upon-Tweed Parliament constituency, represented since May 2015 by Anne-Marie Trevelyan (Conservative), previously held by Alan Beith (Liberal Democrats), and is part of the Rothbury Ward, represented by Steven Christopher Bridgett (Independent). At the parish council level, Alnham is part of Whittingham Parish Council, which includes the former parishes of Alnham, Callaly, and Whittingham. There are seven listed structures in Alnham, including the Church, Tower House, the medieval settlement, and Alnham Castle.

The site contains a sub-circular enclosure within concentric ditches, with ramparts constructed from earth and stone excavated from the hillfort itself. It also includes remains of a Romano-British settlement and at least five hut circles within the hillfort’s interior. Three unenclosed huts on the north-west flanks, defined by a curving out bank, represent the earliest remains and may date back to the Bronze Age. There were four possible phases of development for the earthwork defences during the Iron Age: the first phase involved a univallate stone-walled enclosure, followed by the construction of ramparts and ditches forming a bivallate hillfort (phase 2), while phases 3 and 4 led to Castle Hill becoming a multivallate hillfort. Several trackways near Castle Hill may date from the prehistoric or Romano-British periods, and there is evidence of agricultural activity from the Bronze Age, Iron Age, and Romano-British times. A prehistoric cord rig was found on the north-west of the hilltop, and prehistoric or Romano-British ploughing has created lynchets on the north-east side. Medieval cultivation extended from Alnham village and ceased at a boundary bank on the south-east face of the hill. The most significant 20th-century structure in Alnham is the War Memorial Hall, built in 1920 to reflect the impact of World War I on small rural communities; it is a stone-built village hall with a stone incision above the porch door, and no names are inscribed because there were no village deaths during the war. Alnham is an isolated rural community, with the nearest main road being the A697, approximately 7.5 miles (12 km) away. The village lies on a north-south local road from Prendwick to Scrainwood, and from a junction near the centre, another road heads northwest from Alnham, past Castle Hill, for about 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) to Ewartly Shank, where it ends. In the mid-to-late 19th century, plans existed for a Northumberland Central Railway line to pass through Alnham, positioned to the east of Pennylaws Cottage, but the project was never constructed.
